#10317. Let’s Use the Emergent CSS random() Function in all the Browsers

The creator of the TV show The Good Place wrote a tie-in book about moral philosophy which includes a chapter called “The Luck of the Draw,” discussing how the myth of meritocracy leads people to “underestimate the role that luck has played in their lives.” Given how God seems to play dice with the universe, there is something compelling in the way art imitates life when websites embrace controlled chaos in their designs. The jury is out on whether extreme versions of this nondeterminism such as generative UI are a helpful usage of unpredictable UX. Indeed, when I see the YouTube comments reacting to Google’s upcoming usage of GenUI in search, maybe it’s taking the idea too far down a bad path. But there is still something about the idea of a webpage that exists in a state of subtle flux each time you land on it, the same way you can’t step into the same river twice.

I’m a consultant who often works on short-term, greenfield projects, which provide me with a window into the zeitgeist and the trends companies think are the future. It’s no coincidence that the idea of randomness permeated one of my recent projects. That’s epitomized by a burst of confetti to give the user a sense of excitement when they run a random draw they configured. And like many a UI feature in the corporate world, the simple idea of confetti was subject to several revisions to make every randomized particle align with the client’s brand.

In fact, the requirements became custom enough that we ended up ditching the JavaScript plugin we were using and rolled our own confetti implementation! This illustrates the tension between the conflicting needs for chaos and control in UX, even in a fun feature like random confetti.

Wouldn’t it be nice if we could wield controlled presentational randomness in the presentation layer without leaving CSS?

If unpredictable user experiences are having a moment, it follows that CSS will do its part to make randomized layouts easy to implement. The creators of CSS have always been on a mission to harvest common UI patterns into declarative CSS standards. In keeping with that spirit, we see that in late 2025, Safari became the first browser to support the CSS random() spec, as part of an update that emphasized “letting you solve common use cases with HTML and CSS alone, paving the cowpaths, and reducing the need for JavaScript or third-party frameworks.”

Since then, cool demos and discussions of random() keep popping up. For instance, Schalk Neethling showed us how CSS random() can give us fine-grained control over the infamous confetti effect, and Alvaro Montoro made a strong argument that CSS turns out to be the most suitable language for such tasks. He points out this approach is in line with the Rule of Least Power, which encourages “solving a problem using the least powerful language capable of expressing and solving it.”

Now the bad news: half a year after Safari introduced CSS random(), there isn’t clarity on when it will land in the other browsers. At time of writing, there are signs of life that both Chrome and Firefox have been working on it, but no guarantees about when we will be able to use it outside of the Apple world, even behind a browser flag.

So, it seems currently I can only try the online demos of CSS random() on my work MacBook and not on my PC where I do my personal projects. I am tempted to write my own implementation, but the syntax is surprisingly intricate, mostly because of elaborate random caching and keying semantics, combined with the options for base values and intervals. Even if I could manage to get all those details correct, CSS random() is part of an editor’s draft spec that’s in the “early exploration phase” and “major breaking changes are expected.”

On top of that, from my dive into CSS polyfills in my article on ::nth-letter, we know the whole idea of a CSS polyfill can be a minefield.

With all these obstacles in mind, a person would have to be a special breed of crazy to attempt to polyfill CSS random().

One of the commenters on a neat YouTube demo of the feature marvelled that it’s a “feature that works ONLY IN SAFARI?!? Did the Earth get flipped upside down?” Indeed, I am more accustomed to getting my first opportunity to experience emergent features in Chrome, which means my friends on iPhones often can’t run my experiments.

And yet, in the case of random(), it’s darkly poetic that a feature based on chance appears in an unexpected place where many of us can’t use it. In fact, even Safari users may benefit from my css-random-polyfill package, because Safari updates are tied to the OS, meaning not everyone can upgrade to the latest version of the browser. Besides, we know how much Apple loves it when you hack their stuff to improve compatibility.

Jokes aside, Apple seems serious about the “hackability” and transparency of everything about the open source WebKit engine that powers Safari, and most of the demos I’ve used to test my polyfill are forks of demos from the WebKit blog, in which the Apple Safari team showed off the possibilities for CSS random() back when it was in Safari preview.

Here’s my cross-browser version of the first demo from the Safari team’s article. It’s a randomly scattered field of stars fading in and out at random intervals. The larger, four-pointed stars all tilt at the same randomly selected angle. All stars have subtle, randomly hued shadows around them.

To migrate the Safari-only original to a version that works in Chrome and Firefox, we need to change the HTML to reference my polyfill script and add the randomized marker class to all elements that we want to polyfill.

As for the CSS, unlike my :nth-letter polyfill which uses a nonstandard selector that has to be translated into valid CSS at runtime — and introduces drawbacks in the process — this time we need to support a new function in CSS instead of a new selector. It turns out the CSS we can use in this situation is technically valid, even in browsers that have never heard of CSS random(). More later on why it is valid, but for now, just notice that anywhere we want a random value, we store it in an intermediate custom property, and we always have to follow the convention that the property name starts with the prefix --random.

This starfield demo showcases a few different variations of the supported random() syntax, such as the optional third argument for specifying a step interval which, in this case, is used to randomly select only whole number values within the range:

…and the element-shared base value, which we use here to tilt every four-pointed star by the same randomly selected angle.

Note: In the original starfield demo, most of the random values were used inline, which is admittedly more elegant. The spec that includes random() makes it clear that this kind of function “can be used in place of any part of any property’s value,” just like calc() or min(). So, by requiring extra ceremony and conventions, the polyfill is supporting a subset of what we will get with native random(). To see the glass half-full, it means the CSS stays compatible with the native implementation: we could delete the script reference to the polyfill once native support goes baseline and our code will still work, like it does today when it detects native support in Safari. in this case the polyfill does not process random() calls at all and it lets Safari do all the work. This is a compromise I can live with, especially if the alternative is to press our noses against the glass of Safari-only demos on YouTube and make comments such as one viewer did: “Can’t wait to use this in prod in 4 years.”

Chris Coyier said of the original starfield demo from Apple that he found it “pretty darn compelling!” I agree, and when I was testing my polyfill, that demo was fun to watch randomly twinkling, refresh and see the stars scatter differently using an emergent, declarative CSS standard. By contrast, I can’t say I have ever sat around wishing I could create a 100×100 CSS grid with randomly multicolored cells, so this example from the Safari team feels a bit like a contrived excuse to randomize something. However, it did help me test the polyfill support of a few different variations of the syntax.

The polyfill allows for some flexible syntax. You can see that references to custom properties passed to the random() function get substituted as expected, and you can see that inlining multiple random() calls in the same value works. For example, we can create a grid-area shorthand property value with randomized row-start and column-start values.

This example is from Tim Nguyen from the Safari team. To continue the themes of chance and synchronicity, I’ll mention that I had the good fortune to meet Tim last year when I spoke at Web Directions 2025. My talk came right after his talk, and now that I’m forking his CSS random() demo to create a cross-browser version, he is once again a tough act to follow.

You can see in this example that the final random position of the wheel uses a different unit for its step interval parameter than for the minimum and maximum parameters.

The mix of types is supported because the specs say the values must be “resolvable to the same data type,” so we are able to mix units as long as they are in the same “overall data type,” such as turn and deg, familiar from the way CSS calc() adds values with different units when it makes sense, using CSS typed arithmetic.

Note: To make the demo work with the polyfill, I had to define the variable in a CSS class that will be applied when the polyfill first loads, in contrast to Tim’s original demo which uses the random() function inside a keyframes animation that was applied based on a checkbox hack. That’s because, for now, the polyfill only processes the computed styles that are applied to elements when the page first loads. Since all my tests pass with this implementation, I am leaving it like that for now in the interest of doing the simplest thing that could possibly work. There are ways we could explore to make the polyfill react to dynamic changes to the computed styles and/or the DOM.

Chris Coyier has a knack for writing code that’s either as tricky or as simple as needed to get his point across, and his CodePen “Very basic random() in CSS” is maybe the simplest demo of CSS random() possible, showing three randomly positioned squares with random colors. Below is my cross-browser version, which I also modified to randomize the size of the squares, as a test that my polyfill supports random value sharing using custom keys.

Here is the code I added to make each square have a random height that is equal to its random width:

This reassures that we are supporting the correct syntax. Admittedly, custom keys will be more useful in the real native version, which won’t need the intermediate variables. Since we are using intermediate custom properties, we could just have used one custom property named --side and referenced that for both the height and width values.

Many of the above demos include random colors. That’s achieved by passing random numeric values into CSS color functions such as rgb() or lch(). But if we had a list of specific colors we wanted to randomly choose from, we can’t do that easily, which is why the spec for the CSS values and units module mentions the random-item() function, although no browser currently implements it (except for experimental support in safari preview). If we had this function, we could select a random color or anything else from an arbitrary list of values:

The random-item function takes a mandatory first argument of the type random-caching-options, the same as CSS random(), but then it takes a variable length list of arguments to randomly select from, rather than a minimum and maximum value.

I don’t feel like complicating the polyfill to support a CSS syntax that isn’t implemented in any browser — evidently I only give myself permission to do that once a year. But now that we have a version of CSS random() in Chromium which also supports CSS custom functions and inline conditionals, it’s hard to resist seeing what happens if we combine all these weird and wonderful things into one experiment. It turns out these features together can get us pretty darn close to the functionality we’d get from random-item().

If you’re using a Chromium-based browser, you can see the code in action in this version of the squares demo which sets all three elements to the same color randomly selected from the list.

The implementation of my generic --item custom CSS function takes an --index argument followed by 10 optional arguments. These could be increased to any number of arguments you think will be the realistic maximum size of a collection you would need. Each of the optional arguments is made optional by defaulting it to an empty value, so the caller of the function only needs to pass in the arguments it needs to index. Lastly, the function maps the --index to the argument at that index, because CSS custom functions do not support variable length collections of arguments the way JavaScript functions do.

Sidenote: This generic helper function is interesting, because Temani Afif has demonstrated cool use cases for being able to choose from a list of colors using an --index variable, but the solution he created was specific to the color data type and he freely admits it’s “more of a hack than a CSS feature. So, use it cautiously.” By contrast, the custom function approach will work with a list of any data type, and I wouldn’t describe it as a hack because it’s using CSS standards as intended, albeit emergent standards that aren’t available in all browsers just yet.

Now we have gained confidence in our random() polyfill, you might be curious how it works. Is this a good time to level with you and say I don’t fully know? That’s a very 2026 predicament, but thankfully it’s not because of AI.

As I hinted at the start, my level of eagerness to use new CSS syntax before it’s supported is matched only by my level of laziness to implement and maintain my own version of random(), so I went hunting for an open source JavaScript implementation and was pleasantly surprised it exists!

As you might expect, it’s not designed for the exact purpose I want it for. it’s in an implementation that’s designed to be used at build-time rather than on the client, as a PostCSS plugin. Digging through the source we see that this plugin wraps the MIT-licensed @csstools/css-calc which has no dependencies and isn’t coupled to PostCSS. The Readme for this package says it only implements the older CSS Values and Units Module Level 4, but we see from the commit history that it’s recently had an “update to latest spec” of random() and we see it passing automated tests for the kind of random goodness we have been enjoying in this article.

My main question is how on earth we are going to hook it up to client-side CSS, but it turns out not to be too much custom code:

Let’s translate this code into natural language steps:

Point 4 is a big deal. Interpreting arbitrary custom property values using CSS is the closest we have in present day CSS to an honest-to-goodness documented extension point for the language. Since arbitrary expressions in custom variable values are valid and can be read by JavaScript via the computed styles, this approach has the potential to avoid many of the known downsides of polyfilling CSS such as refetching and rewriting stylesheets, doing our own parsing of CSS, and other fun but dangerous pastimes.

Fittingly, it’s only by good luck that an open source project has already done most of the work we need to be able to run CSS random() in any browser while we wait for native support. A lot of people claim they can’t wait for this feature to be available in more browsers, so it will be interesting to see whether people choose to wait now that a polyfill exists. Seeing Chris Coyier’s reaction to the starfield demo, his enthusiasm was contagious! I had a similar moment when I first got the demo working in other browsers. Let me know if having this polyfill available sparks creativity for your own projects. I definitely have ideas for some more advanced use cases for it, which is what prompted me to polyfill it.

Till next time, happy randomizing from your friendly neighbourhood random guy.

#10315. Pixel Watch update brings a sweet redesign I wish was on more apps

Google has been at its gradient redesign schtick for a while now to varying levels of success, but its latest redesign has just landed on the Pixel Watch for the Media Controls app, and I love it.

Quietly rolled out, the Media Controls app on Pixel Watch has picked up a redesign to its app icon, adopting the same gradient look we’ve seen across several other Pixel Watch apps.

The difference here is that Google’s styling expands beyond a simple coat of paint. The new look extends to the edge of the icon with play/pause in the center and a ring indicating playback around the border, just like the actual app itself – the app, to be clear, hasn’t been redesigned.

I’ve personally been a bit mixed on these redesigns, but this one really nails it in my book. I wish Google would do this sort of thing more often. The white borders are nice in some cases, but I very much miss the whimsy of the icons that took up the full size available to them – that mid-2010’s icon was the absolute peak in my opinion.

Pixel Watch has been quietly rolling out more of these icon redesigns in recent months, with the other most recent additions including Alarm, Stopwatch, and Timer from around August/September.

#10310. Data-Driven Pages That Never Go Stale: A Practical Guide

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every developer has shipped the other kind of page: a lovingly written article or landing page that peaks on launch day and then quietly rots. Screenshots age, statistics expire, rankings slide. Data-driven pages play the opposite game. Built from a living dataset, they republish themselves daily, grow to thousands of URLs, and answer questions nobody had asked when the site launched. This guide breaks down how they work, using a real fan-run stats site as the running example: one public dataset in, more than ten thousand fresh pages out.

Static pages lose ground because the web moves and they do not. Facts expire, competitors publish fresher answers, and search engines reward pages whose information matches today. A page that cannot update itself must be rewritten by hand, so most sites update a few pages and abandon the rest.

Freshness is not one rule for the whole web; it depends on the query. Nobody needs a CSS tutorial rewritten weekly, but statistics, prices, availability and anything with a season attached decays on a schedule. Developers misjudge this constantly, treating every page like documentation when half their catalogue is really a perishable good. Serve a three-month-old stat as if it were current and readers learn the most damaging lesson a site can teach: do not trust the numbers here.

Then there is the maintenance maths. A hundred hand-written pages each needing one review a year is a hundred small debts, and the interest compounds as the catalogue grows. The team updates the flagship pages, promises to return for the rest, and quietly never does. Data-driven architecture is really a staffing decision disguised as a technical one: humans design the system once, and the system does the updating forever.

A data-driven site has three layers: a dataset that refreshes on a schedule, templates that turn records into pages, and URL patterns that map every meaningful combination users might search for. Change the data and every page changes; improve a template and ten thousand pages improve at once.

The running example makes this concrete. A fan-built Overwatch stats tracker republishes Blizzard's public hero data on a daily cycle. From that one feed it generates hero profiles, head-to-head matchup pages and multi-condition tier lists: 10,291 URLs in its sitemap, across six languages, with matchup pages alone accounting for 8,586 of them. Nobody wrote those pages. Somebody designed the system that writes them, which is a very different, and much more scalable, job.

The example runs on Next.js behind a CDN, but the stack is the least important layer of the three. The same pipeline feeding WordPress, Astro or a static site generator would look identical from the reader's side of the glass. Choose boring technology you already know, and spend your originality budget on the dataset and the templates, because that is where readers will feel the difference.

Generated pages stay useful when every URL must earn its existence with data. Set minimum thresholds before a page is published, give each template unique modules its siblings do not have, and noindex combinations with nothing to say. The line between a resource and spam is not automation; it is emptiness.

Quality gates work best when they are public and mechanical. The example site publishes its tier formula openly: 70% of the score from win rate, 30% from pick rate, and a hard floor that excludes heroes picked in under 0.5% of matches from topping the ranking, because a tiny sample cannot prove anything. That single floor is editorial policy expressed as code. Your version might be a minimum number of data points, a minimum price history, or a minimum review count — the number matters less than the fact that the gate exists and applies to every page equally.

Each template also needs modules its siblings cannot copy. A hero profile carries a seven-day trend and its best and worst matchups; a matchup page carries the head-to-head history; a tier list carries the movement since yesterday. Add a short human layer on top — a methodology page explaining the scoring, changelogs narrating what moved — and the catalogue stops reading as output and starts reading as a publication. Google's scaled-content rules target pages manufactured to manipulate rankings with little value; a page that answers a real query with real, current data is the opposite of that. The honest test for any generated URL is simple: if it vanished tonight, would a searcher lose an answer?

Start embarrassingly small: one dataset, one entity type, one template. A football club's results archive, a property portal's sold prices, your own product catalogue — anything structured and refreshed beats a grand plan. Prove one template earns traffic, then add combinations, languages and dashboards in that order.

What is programmatic SEO? Programmatic SEO means generating many pages from a structured dataset using templates, instead of writing each page by hand. Done well, each page answers a distinct search with real data. Done badly, it produces thousands of near-identical pages, which is where its reputation suffers.

Is programmatic SEO against Google's rules? No. Google's spam policies target scaled content created mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value for users. Pages generated from real data that answer real queries are publishing. The deciding question is whether a page helps its reader, not how it was produced.

How often should the data behind pages refresh? Match the refresh to how fast the underlying facts change. Sports and game statistics justify daily pulls, prices often need hourly checks, and reference data may only move monthly. Refreshing faster than reality changes wastes crawl budget and makes 'updated' stamps meaningless.

Do generated pages need unique written text? They need unique value, which is not the same thing. Identical paragraphs on ten thousand pages add nothing, but unique data, comparisons and trends are content in their own right. Add short human-written context per template, and let the data carry the differences between pages.

How many pages should a first project launch with? Launch with the smallest set that proves the template: one entity type, a few hundred pages at most. Validate that search engines index them and users engage before adding combinations and languages. Scaling an unproven template just manufactures tomorrow's cleanup job at industrial size.

The sites quietly winning the long game are not publishing more; they are publishing systems. One honest dataset, one well-built template and strict quality gates will outlast a hundred hand-written pages competing on freshness alone. Try it this week: take one dataset you already own, design a single template with four real modules, and ship fifty pages. Watch what the data does next.

#10301. Running WireGuard for a Development Team: The Hidden Cost of VPN Maintenance

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Setting up WireGuard on a small virtual server is a satisfying infrastructure task. Install the package, generate a key pair, open a UDP port, configure a peer, and connect a laptop. Within an afternoon, your staging environment can sit behind a private tunnel, and your internal dashboard can be restricted to traffic from a known address.

The initial setup is rarely the difficult part.

The real engineering work starts when the team changes. A developer joins, another leaves, someone replaces a laptop, a server needs patching, or a connection suddenly stops working. Each event creates a small maintenance task. Over time, those tasks become an operational responsibility that somebody must own.

This article examines what it takes to operate a self-hosted WireGuard VPN for a development team. We'll look at peer configuration, access management, troubleshooting, monitoring tools, and the engineering time involved. We'll also compare self-hosting with managed business VPN services so teams can make a decision based on their infrastructure needs.

WireGuard is a modern VPN protocol designed to establish encrypted connections between network peers. Its relatively small codebase, modern cryptography, and straightforward configuration make it attractive for developers who want control over their network infrastructure.

A basic WireGuard deployment typically involves:

A server with a reachable public IP address.

A private and public key pair for the server.

A UDP port through which peers communicate.

Peer configuration that defines which addresses are allowed through the tunnel.

A simplified server configuration might look like this:

The corresponding client configuration contains the client's private key and the server's public key:

These examples illustrate the basic relationship between a server and a client. A production configuration will also need appropriate firewall rules, routing, DNS settings, and a plan for distributing configuration securely.

The important distinction is that WireGuard establishes encrypted peer connections. It does not automatically provide a complete employee identity system, onboarding workflow, approval process, or audit dashboard.

Those responsibilities belong to the team operating the infrastructure.

Developers interested in using WireGuard on personal development devices can also explore SitePoint's guide to building a hardened mobile development environment with Termux, Docker, and WireGuard.

A peer is not just an entry in a configuration file. It represents a device that has permission to communicate through your network.

That makes peer management an access-control responsibility.

For a small development team, it is tempting to keep a single configuration file and update it manually whenever someone joins or leaves. This can work initially, but it becomes harder to manage as the number of devices increases.

A useful first step is to maintain a peer inventory:

The inventory should not contain private keys. Private keys must remain on their respective devices and should never be placed in a shared spreadsheet or source repository.

The inventory instead helps administrators answer practical questions:

Which device is associated with this tunnel address?

Has the peer been removed after the device was lost or replaced?

This information becomes especially important when a team uses the VPN to reach staging servers, internal dashboards, databases, or other development resources.

Manual onboarding is manageable when a team has only two or three developers. It becomes unreliable when several people join, leave, or change devices over the year.

A repeatable onboarding process should cover more than generating a key pair.

Confirm that the team member is authorized to access the environment.

Generate a key pair on the user's device.

Add the public key to the server's peer configuration.

Apply the appropriate routing and firewall permissions.

Deliver the client configuration through a secure channel.

Test access to the specific development resources the person needs.

Record the peer owner, device, and approval details.

Offboarding needs an equally clear process:

Identify every peer associated with the departing team member.

Remove the relevant public keys from the server.

Confirm that the configuration change has been applied.

Review any other credentials or allowlists that granted access.

An administrator can inspect the currently configured peers with:

The output helps identify peer public keys, transfer counters, and latest handshake information. It is useful for troubleshooting, but it should not be treated as a complete access audit or proof that a particular person is still authorized.

The broader lesson is to make access changes part of a documented workflow. A peer should not remain active simply because nobody remembers who created it.

One common network-design mistake is assuming that connecting to a VPN should give a developer access to every internal service.

A developer working on a frontend application may need access to a staging web server but not to the production database. A contractor may need access to one test environment without being able to reach internal administration tools.

WireGuard's peer configuration and the surrounding network controls should be designed around those requirements.

Separate tunnel address ranges for different groups.

Firewall rules that restrict traffic to approved services.

Cloud security groups that limit access to specific ports.

Application-level authentication for internal dashboards.

Separate production and staging network boundaries.

The exact implementation depends on the infrastructure. The key point is that VPN membership and application authorization are different controls.

A successful VPN handshake should not be treated as permission to access every resource behind the tunnel.

A VPN can appear simple when it works. Diagnosing it becomes more complicated when a developer is connecting from a home router, a hotel network, or a mobile hotspot.

Incorrect routing or AllowedIPs settings.

A server process or host becoming unavailable.

WireGuard provides useful inspection commands:

These commands help inspect peer information, check the service state, and review recent service logs. The exact systemd service name can differ depending on how the interface was configured.

Administrators should also monitor the underlying server. At minimum, that means checking:

Whether the WireGuard interface is active.

Whether disk or memory usage is approaching a limit.

Whether operating-system and package updates are pending.

A small virtual server may be inexpensive, but it is still infrastructure that needs an owner.

Teams working with alternative tunnel-based development workflows may find SitePoint's tutorial on setting up Cloudflare Tunnels with Docker Compose for persistent webhook debugging useful. It covers a different tunneling use case, but the operational questions around connectivity, service health, and troubleshooting are closely related.

A self-hosted VPN does not need to become a collection of manual tasks. A few established tools can make configuration, monitoring, and debugging more repeatable.

The core tool is, of course, WireGuard. Its command-line utilities allow administrators to inspect peers, manage interfaces, and review connection information. The official documentation is the best starting point for understanding configuration options and platform support.

Ansible can automate repeatable server administration tasks. A team could use playbooks to deploy configuration files, apply system updates, or standardize firewall settings across several VPN hosts.

Sensitive values should be handled with an appropriate secrets-management approach. Private keys should not be committed to a Git repository or stored in plaintext playbooks.

Prometheus is useful for collecting and querying metrics, while Node Exporter exposes Linux host metrics such as CPU, memory, disk, and network statistics.

These tools do not automatically provide a complete WireGuard security audit. They can, however, help identify resource problems and server-health issues before those problems become user-reported outages.

Uptime Kuma provides a self-hosted monitoring dashboard with notifications. It can help teams monitor the availability of a VPN host or related services.

A basic availability check does not prove that every VPN peer can connect successfully. For more meaningful monitoring, combine host checks with an end-to-end test from a separate network.

Wireshark and tcpdump help developers inspect network traffic when diagnosing connectivity problems.

For example, tcpdump can capture UDP traffic on the WireGuard port:

This can help determine whether packets are reaching the server. It does not decrypt WireGuard traffic or replace checks of routing, firewall rules, and peer configuration.

The right toolset depends on the size of the deployment. A team with one VPN server may only need WireGuard's own commands and basic host monitoring. A larger environment may benefit from automation, centralized metrics, and a documented incident process.

A self-hosted VPN can cost very little in direct infrastructure charges. However, the server invoice does not include the engineering time required to operate it.

Consider a hypothetical team with these assumptions:

Two people join and two leave during the year.

The team reviews or rotates device keys quarterly.

Patching and monitoring require about two hours per month.

Six troubleshooting incidents occur annually.

The estimated loaded engineering cost is $60 per hour.

The virtual server costs approximately $6 per month.

The following estimate illustrates how quickly maintenance time can exceed the infrastructure bill.

At $60 per hour, 46 hours represent approximately $2,760 in engineering time. The server adds around $72 per year, bringing the estimated total to $2,832.

These figures are illustrative, not a universal cost benchmark. A team with infrastructure automation and established monitoring may spend considerably less time. A team with frequent staff changes or strict audit requirements may spend more.

The useful exercise is to measure the work your own team performs. Track onboarding, access reviews, patching, incidents, and recovery time for a few months. That gives you a more realistic comparison than looking at hosting prices alone.

Self-hosting is not automatically the best option just because a team has developers who can configure servers.

A managed business VPN may be worth considering when the team needs centralized member management, simpler device administration, or a stable network exit address without maintaining the underlying VPN infrastructure.

Depending on the provider and plan, managed services may offer:

A central dashboard for adding and removing users.

Client applications for common operating systems.

Multi-factor authentication or identity integrations.

For example, PureVPN for Teams is one service in this category. Teams evaluating it—or any other provider—should check the current feature set, pricing, logging practices, access controls, and service terms before making a decision.

A managed service does not remove every security responsibility. The team still needs to decide who receives access, review permissions, protect user accounts, and understand how traffic and metadata are handled.

It also introduces vendor dependency and a recurring subscription cost. Those trade-offs should be considered alongside the engineering time saved.

There are situations where running WireGuard yourself is the more practical option.

You already operate infrastructure. If your team routinely patches servers, manages secrets, monitors services, and responds to incidents, maintaining a VPN may add relatively little work.

You need custom routing. A deployment that connects several private cloud networks, on-premises environments, or specialized subnets may require network controls that are easier to implement directly.

You have strict data-control requirements. Some organizations have policies that limit which third parties can handle network traffic or related metadata. Those requirements may favor infrastructure under the organization's own control.

You have a dedicated platform or security team. If someone is explicitly responsible for access management, monitoring, and incident response, self-hosting can fit naturally into existing operations.

You can automate the lifecycle. Infrastructure-as-code, configuration management, documented peer inventories, and tested recovery procedures can reduce repetitive work and make a self-hosted deployment easier to maintain.

The important distinction is between a deliberately operated service and a one-off server that nobody owns.

Before choosing an approach, ask the following questions:

Who is responsible for the VPN six or twelve months after deployment?

How many people and devices are likely to join or leave?

How are public keys and peer configurations tracked?

How quickly can access be revoked when a device is lost?

Which internal services should each developer be able to reach?

Do you need a fixed egress IP for external allowlists?

What monitoring and recovery process exists if the server fails?

Do your customers or internal policies require access logs or formal reviews?

Does your team have the time and expertise to maintain the infrastructure?

Would a managed service cost less than the engineering time and operational risk it replaces?

If your team already has mature infrastructure practices and needs custom network control, self-hosting may be a sensible choice.

If the team is small, access changes frequently, and nobody has time to own another server, a managed service may be more practical.

WireGuard is an excellent protocol, and deploying it can be a straightforward engineering task. But operating a VPN for a development team involves more than establishing an encrypted connection.

Peer management, onboarding, offboarding, network permissions, monitoring, patching, and troubleshooting all require ongoing attention.

The right choice depends on the team's infrastructure experience, security requirements, size, and available engineering time. Self-hosting offers control and flexibility; a managed service can reduce operational work. Neither option removes the need for sound access-control practices.

Before deciding, calculate the maintenance effort, identify who will own the service, and make sure the design can be maintained as the team changes.

The cost example uses illustrative assumptions rather than current vendor pricing. Managed VPN features and prices can change, so verify provider details before purchasing.

#10298. CSS-Tricks has a new owner!

This is pretty wild, but let’s get right to it because it’s big news:

CSS-Tricks is an independent site once again!

Just to recap: DigitalOcean purchased CSS-Tricks in 2022 from Chris Coyier, who founded the site in 2007. Chris ran it all the way up to that purchase.

Here we are in 2026, and I’m taking independent ownership of the site.

So, wait, who owns the site? That’d be me. (Wow, never imagined I would get to say that!) Of course, I have a small, awesome team to help with the day-to-day management of the site.

That all said, I do envision that some things will change. In fact, I’m planning that they will change in what I hope are very good ways. Maybe a question-answer thing makes sense here since this is very much an evolving discussion.

Yes, I’ve got the keys to the castle, so to speak. And, even after 12 years of working on the site, I’ll admit I’m a little overwhelmed and nervous about that. I mean, it’s an investment for sure, as you can imagine, and I’m making this my full-time job. At least for a while.

I want to make CSS-Tricks both a real community and a place that’s inclusive of everyone, no matter where they are in their front-end learning journey. That’s going to take some work and time.

My latest IPO launched, and I’m now worth one trillion dollars. Wait, wait. That’s not right.

It’s going to be hard. Advertising will certainly be needed now. But, in order to keep the lights on, I’ll have to approach them differently.

In the pre-DigitalOcean days we sold real ad packages with things like display ads, sponsored posts, newsletter sponsors, and the like. As an independent website, we will need to return to our advertising roots.

So, if you’re in a place looking to advertise, please do reach out!

Right?! Ad revenue can’t be the only thing paying the bills. I have lots of ideas and several plates already spinning. Like, I’ve been neck deep in developing an HTML/CSS course for beginners.

(And you can now support the site by becoming a member — thanks in advance!)

Educational content has been in the dumps lately, right? Again, I’m hoping that CSS-Tricks will be more inclusive, no matter where you or anyone else is at in the learning journey. This place has traditionally been for folks who know what they’re doing. But I’m truly committed to creating more entry points for those getting started, particularly as our field is in the early throes of a growing skills gap.

And yes, I do believe that learning the basics is more important now than ever. But what learning actually looks like is what’s key. Front-end courses are down across the board. It has to be done differently.

There are other things in the works, but I think a course is one of the first things you’ll see.

Oh, and the newsletter. That’s coming back after a way-too-long hiatus.

That’s still very much a thing! We’ll keep our regularly scheduled broadcast going.

But maybe a little less than you’re used to. Those articles are part of the investment I’m making. Expect maybe one or two articles most weeks, at least as the ball starts rolling.

That also means the guest writing form is back in business! We have a nice backlog of articles through the rest of the year, which is great, but also means new submissions will have to wait a bit.

I won’t be able to accept everything that comes in, but I will absolutely read them and follow-up as best I can. Unless it’s a slop submission, of course.

Nah! My goal is to make CSS-Tricks a platform that gives folks a voice to share great ideas. I think we all prefer that over me just using it as my own soapbox. I’ve written plenty for this site the past 12 years. I’m happier (and more comfortable) being behind the curtain and giving others the full spotlight.

I may be writing a bit, developing the site here and there, editing a small stack of article drafts, or helping with sponsorships. I gag at the thought of titles, but publisher hits best for me. My fingers are in all the bowls, but my most important responsibilities are:

The best thing I can possibly do is help folks develop a voice and give them a stage to use it. It’s about community and culture building. Publisher. That’s more my jam.

You totally can. I put a little membership deal together where you can join a members-only community on Discord along with some perks. Or check out the new shop. Or purchase advertising for your company. In the near-future you will be able to purchase the aforementioned course as well. Any little bit helps, of course. I squirm at the thought of asking for money, so there’s no pressure.

Support doesn’t even have to be financial! We all know that content publishers need all the eyeballs we can get in these prompt-filled days. Things like subscribing to the newsletter, sharing articles you like with others, clicking through from your RSS app, and checking out our sponsors are all very, very great ways to support us.

Yeah, me too. This post could go on and on. I’m an open book, though, and I’m happy to answer anything you might have in the comments. I know, so 2015, right?

Andy Clarke shows you how to create designs that people recognize and remember in his brand-new e-book, Standout Designs for the Web. Pre-order it today!

Hurrah!! Thank you for all your work on CSS Tricks and for stewarding it into a new era! Excited to see what’s to come :)

Couldn’t agree more. Starting a business is definitely a risky decision when the economy is down. Hang in there!

I am so happy for this news! As someone who used to help support ad sales for CSS-Tricks pre-DigitalOcean days, this is great news. The site deserved way more attention than it got and I’m glad that it’s in the hands of someone that cares about the content and the community.

First of all: congrats! It’s clear the DO did not have a vision for this site, so I’m happy that they released ownership.

Second, and I mean this with the best intentions I read you’re planning to have external people write articles. That’s fine, and honestly I don’t care who the source is, as long as the article is informative and well-written. I’ve often felt not only the quantity, but also the quality had dropped since even before the acquisition.

It’s always a fine line balancing between writing for both junior and senior profiles, so I don’t envy your position. I wish you luck and I hope the site can survive the current LLM-filled landscape.

Congrats, Geoff! Looking forward to seeing where things go from here!

Congratulations Geoff! Love the site. Nothing can replicate your human ingenuity and style!!

Huge! I learnt almost everything I know about advanced CSS here over the years, a lot of that went into my forum software. Which, given you’re going community focused I’d love to see if you’re interested in using, I’d be happy to host and collaborate!

This is amazing. I stopped coming after some time because it seemed DO just ignored this place altogether. Guess it’s time to start coming back.

So happy that this came to fruition Geoff – you’ve been such a strong advocate for and leader of CSS Tricks for so long, and it’s great to see it fully in your hands! I know you’ll do great things with it.

Never knew the shop was there before. Any chance of a mouse matt with the CSS tricks logo instead of just a mouse pad? I want to be able to put both my keyboard and mouse on it and I’m almost in the market for a new one.

It’s like owning a classic car but it’s not just a classic. It’s past, present and the future! Congrats, Geoff! This is so cool!

It is tricky to even express how glad I am to have CSS-Tricks back under independent ownership. Just having into the hands of people who care rather than a corporation that doesn’t means so much.

I’m sure it won’t be easy – the industry is in a tumultuous state – but it will be of such great value and meaning. I look forward to the new era.

This is like the one of brightest rays of light in a sea of bleak moments of the year 2026 Awesome to see CSS Tricks not slowly drowning anymore!

This is such fantastic news, congrats! I’m excited to see where it goes.

Many hopes that this could become a place of quality and curation in this time of slop.

This is incredible! Best news of the day! Well done and good winds. ☺️

Yesssss. So happy for this (and you!) In this era, we need high quality curated educational content more than ever. We’re living in a world where LLMs learn from all the bad practice out there, and can only tell us all things all at once. We need the knowledgeable folks to guide us through what’s worth learning, cut through hype, and craft learning experiences in a way that only humans (like Geoff) can.

Great news! Hope it all works out for you.

Congratulations, excited to see what y’all do!

So cool! One of the best websites is back again!

This is exciting, operating at a smaller scale is good.

Advertising the way you’ve described is fine by me, actually. Ads that don’t track you, that are pertinent to the audience, and that don’t block content are not offensive to me. Gotta keep the lights on somehow. (Sponsorships are good, too, but certainly aren’t always sufficient.)

Congratulations. CSS-Tricks was a big part of my early journey and still gets a visit from time to time. Looking forward to the future.

Wow, congrats! Maybe not the first-first change but… css-tricks needs a redesign, you know it, right? It used to change so often back in the days! Anyway, congrats again!!

It’ll get little iterations here and there, that’s for sure. :)

So cool! Congrats. This will be a fun new era.

these are the best news i heard in a long time godspeed

It’s been quite possibly the toughest period ever for educators and a big win like this really does change the game. Let’s all hope the momentum from this win can put CSS-Tricks back where it deserves to be and hopefully, beyond.

Huge congratulations, Geoff. Publisher-to-publisher, this was the only right route because you simply are the best in the biz. We’ll do everything we can do to help over at Piccalilli too.

Congratulations and good luck, Geoff! CSS-Tricks has been a big part of my learning and contributing journey, and I’m grateful to have been part of its community. Excited to see this new chapter under your leadership!

Heck yeah and congrats all around!! This is great news for the entire community. Will definitely check out the various links on how we can support this new chapter!

Great news, looking forward to seeing the revival!

The internet may thrive again. Congratulations Geoff! One step away from the encroaching darkness we progress.

Congrats, and all the best wishes! I’ve been following this site for years and found it highly helpful. In my earlier days, i was following the Opera blog thing for the latest and greatest, then I had an extended hiatus when opera moved away from Presto, and then I came back to web in 2020. This site has made catching up, learning, and reflecting on Web, Web accessibility, CSS, and more so much more enjoyable!

First last.fm, now CSS-Tricks. That is incredible news—congratulations, Geoff, and all the best moving forward!

Wow. That’s great news. I’m curious to see how CSS-Tricks will evolve, and I’ll be keeping my fingers crossed. I’ve really missed having CSS-Tricks as an independent site.

Congrats on the new ownership chapter. Exciting to see CSS-Tricks keep evolving with the community that grew up around it.

It’s great to see CSS-Tricks returning to independent ownership! A strong web development community depends on practical knowledge, experienced contributors and quality resources that help people continuously improve their skills. I particularly appreciate the focus on making the platform more inclusive for beginners while continuing to support experienced developers. Looking forward to seeing how the community and content evolve under the new ownership. Wishing Geoff and the team every success with this new chapter!

#10296. Motorola MA2 wireless Android Auto adapter just vanished days after finally going on sale

The long-awaited Motorola MA2 wireless Android Auto adapter is gone just days after it went on sale.

Motorola MA2 is a wireless Android Auto adapter designed with Google. It was announced way back in March 2026 as the sequel to MA1, which itself launched back in 2022. Needless to say, it’s debut has been long-awaited, and that arrived earlier this week.

But, just as quickly as it came, it’s gone.

We noticed today that Motorola MA2 has vanished on Amazon. The listing is still live, but doesn’t appear in search and is completely sold out. You can try your luck, but odds are it’ll be out of stock for a little while to come.

This isn’t a huge surprise. The listing showed a delivery date in mid-late December, implying that stock hasn’t hit Amazon’s warehouses just yet. It’s not particularly uncommon for listings like these to be taken down briefly as stock is on its way.

More than likely, MA2 will return sometime in the next few weeks. Stay tuned, we’ll be keeping a close eye on it!

#10294. The UGREEN HomeAgent is a ‘local-first’ way to make your smart home even smarter

Smart home tech often relies solely on cloud connections and pricey AI subscriptions, but UGREEN is delivering a local-first solution in its new HomeAgent collection, delivering cameras, speakers, and more that bring the bulk of the functionality and processing directly to your home.

The UGREEN AIoT – AI of Things – ecosystem is built around pairing hardware to a central hub that acts as your home’s brain. The HomeAgent HA100 and Pro are that “brain,” pairing to smart home gear such as lights, speakers, and cameras to not only store recordings, but process the data locally.

At the core of the experience is UGREEN’s Uliya AI assistant, which you can talk to directly through HomeAgent HA100 or through a connected Smart Speaker for Uliya. The assistant can handle simple tasks like controlling lights or playing music, of course, but can do a lot more with video recordings. You can ask questions such as “is there a package outside” or “where is my dog” and Uliya will be able to parse through camera recordings to find the answer rather than forcing you to have to scroll through timelines.

That’s all powered by the HomeAgent HA100. It can also acts as network storage for photos, household files, and more, all of which can be used as context for the local AI system – and there’s no monthly fee to store or access it.

UGREEN’s hardware lineup around the HomeAgent centerpieces includes cameras such as the SynCare cameras. These deliver the local recording capabilities that are so central to the system. SynCare OD800 Pro is a triple-lens outdoor camera with solar power and a built-in battery, while the OD600 Pro delivers the same powerful camera setup with power-over-ethernet. These have an 8MP primary camera and dual 5MP cameras with pan-tilt-zoom capabilities. They can zoom in up to 9x, feature motion tracking and a built-in spotlight, as well as color night vision and IP66 dust/water protection.

There are also two smart frames, the UGREEN Gallery E-Paper Smart Frame mounts on the wall to display photos and artwork, while the UGREEN Gallery LCD Smart Frame can sit on a table or hang on the wall, showing photos and videos, while also integrating with the rest of your smart home’s functions.

UGREEN has its own smart speaker for the system, and you can also integrate select Matter hardware as well, including smart lighting, robot vacuums and other smart home devices.

The UGREEN HomeAgent ecosystem will start at $799 for a limited time when its Kickstarter campaign launches on April 13, 2027, with upgraded packages that drastically increase AI processing power, storage, and the types of devices you can connect to the system.

You can reserve your UGREEN HomeAgent today to lock in early bird pricing. Reservations are open from September 4, 2026, through April 12, 2027, and deposits can be canceled for a refund any time before the campaign ends. Shipping will begin in late June 2027, with different phases for different products.
